data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a non-inductive 'conventional decision' to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby maximizing the informational content of our errors should we fail.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration is interpreted as assigning a higher logical probability of truth to the theory, the defense collapses into the induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent requires a guarantee of practical safety (e.g., bridge stability) rather than a willingness to learn from potential failure, Popperian preference is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory logically entails believing it is approximately true (verisimilitude) in a way that can be calculated, the formal undefined nature of verisimilitude undermines the rational basis for the choice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Severity-Based Conventionalism: The preference is a methodological rule (a convention) rather than a logical derivation. It selects the theory that offers the highest empirical content and has survived the strictest tests, ensuring that if the theory is false, the resulting practical failure will be most informative for subsequent conjecture. This avoids induction because it makes no claim about the probability of future success, only about the current status of the theory regarding past tests.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
